utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. May the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Welcome to everybody and may we please get the appearances the parties, please. Prosecutor, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. Alan Tieger and Laurie Sartorio, with case manager Donnica Henry Frijlink for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Greg Kehoe and Luka Misetic for General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For the Defence of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. General Cermak is represented by myself, Cedo Prodanovic, and my colleague, Ms. Jadranka Slokovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prodanovic. And for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence for General Markac is myself, Miroslav Separovic around Mr. Goran Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we proceed, can we just make sure that General Gotovina and General Markac and General Cermak can hear us in a language they understand. General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Everything is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And General Markac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MARKAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just by way of a preliminary remark to explain the apparent awkward sitting of the Bench, the only reason that I'm sitting in the centre here is because I'm Pre-Trial Judge in this matter, most probably going to sit as the Trial Judge. It is not quite certain that either Judge Orie or Judge Van Den Wyngaert would sit, and that's the only reason that I'm sitting in the centre. The last Status Conference in the present case was held on the 5th of December, 2006; and pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Status Conference shall be convened within 120 days of the last, in order to organise exchanges between the parties, to ensure the expeditious preparation for trial, and to allow the accused to raise issues in the case. Given today's major agenda items, the alleged conflicts of interests between the various Defence teams and Mr. Cermak's compliance with the conditions of his provisional release, the full Bench is present. And earlier this afternoon, a 65 ter meeting was held with the parties and the senior legal officer of the Trial Chamber I, in preparation for the present hearing. May we just deal, first of all, with the situation on the health of the accused. General Gotovina, do you have anything to say about your own health and conditions of stay in the UNDU?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for asking me. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General Gotovina. General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Cermak. The interpreters could not hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my health is just fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General Markac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MARKAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you know that my health is not good, but the team of doctors is doing their best to reduce my pain or improve my health if that is at all possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General Markac. The next item I would like to deal with is the rule 93 bis (D) situation. In its response to the Trial Chamber's request pursuant to Rule 73 bis (D) filed on the 22nd of January this year, the Prosecution stated it was not fully able to consider any possible overlap between the counts, because the Defence has filed a motion seeking to strike certain counts from the joinder indictment. So any discussion of cumulative charging would be premature at this stage until a decision has been issued. Am I capturing the situation of the Prosecution correctly, Mr. Tieger, on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On that particular point, Your Honour, I believe so. I'm not sure if the Chamber is directing its attention to the entirety of the motion or seek some clarification on that single point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, not at all. I just wanted to be sure we have captured you correctly. And you said that in order to do so, the Prosecution would reduce its case by reducing the number of municipalities in the indictment by six and reduce the temporal scope by two months. You also said it was premature to indicate what impact such decision would have on the number of witnesses it may call since the 65 ter witness list is not here completed or submitted. At this point the Chamber is inclined then to order the Prosecution to reduce the indictment as they indicated, and the Trial Chamber reserves the right to review the indictment further and order for more reductions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. The anticipated order was mentioned at the 65 ter conference, and I understand the nature of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So the Prosecution is so ordered to reduce the indictment accordingly. The next item is the question of agreed facts. What progress has been made in that direction? May we start with you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was extensive discussion with respect to this particular aspect of trial preparation at the 65 ter. I can only summarise it briefly, I trust, by indicating that although there have been continuing discussions, we -- I think there was a consensus between the Prosecution and the Defence that in light of the necessary steps to achieve meaningful progress on meaningful agreed facts, there's going to be considerable difficulty in light of the competing demands on both the Prosecution and the Defence between at least now and the submission of the Defence pre-trial brief and which leaves precious little time between than point and trial, much of which I anticipate will be spent at least by the Prosecution in making necessary arrangements and preparation for the commencement of trial. So we have not abandoned that effort. Indeed, Defence counsel and I met into the early evening hours yesterday to pursue that, but the reality is that that effort made clear to us, as it has before, the nature of the process and the steps it requires, including among three Defence teams considerable logistical coordination and contact with their individual clients. And although we will not consciously abandon it, we're not very optimistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did I understand you to be saying that the Defence counsel has logistical problems in contacting their clients?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour. Well, I mean -- what I'm suggesting is that for every step forward, that cannot proceed, as I understand it, from their side - and they're welcome to explain it further themselves - without exchange between counsel and then subsequent contact with the individual clients. I am suggesting that that is a logistical aspect to the nature of agreed facts that plays a significant role in any effort to move forward, but I didn't mean suggest that there are any unusual logistical impediments. Maybe there are, but they'd have to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was the Defence counsel that has been interfacing with Mr. Tieger for the most part on the agreed facts, but the reality is, Judge, with the accelerated trial schedule of May 7th, a meaningful discussion on agreed facts -- there is simply no time for any meaningful discussion on agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's just get things correct here. When you say accelerated schedule, what was it before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I believe that there was notification from the Registry that trial was to be in January of 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's water under the bridge, Mr. Kehoe. We've discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge, but I'm just discussing where we are vis-a-vis agreed facts with the reduced time schedule that we have to prepare this case and to deal with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There has never been a scheduling for January 2008, so there cannot be talk of reduced scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With all due respect, Judge, I do believe a notification came out of the Registry that the Registry was looking at this trial for January of 2008. With all due respect, Judge, I do believe that that was communicated publicly. That being said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have -- are you able to give us a copy of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't have it personally, but that's my understanding from co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- this is again a public statement that was made by the spokesman for the Prosecutor's office. As I understand it, from A, my counsel and for Mr. Cermak; and B, from the Prosecution, subsequent to the last time we were at a Status Hearing, that information came as part of a schedule that the Registry had put together on what the approximate trial times were. So whether that is from this -- I think we were advised in the 65 ter conference in December that there is a committee of the Judges that makes scheduling plans for which case are going to go to trial when, and that that committee decided that we were prepared to go to trial and that, therefore, we should now be ready to go to trial in May of 2007. It was our assumption after that fact, that it was that same committee through the Registry that had approximated the trial dates be in early 2008, but we are talking about information that has been given to Defence counsel for Cermak and, apparently, the spokesman for the Prosecutor's office said that was the trial date. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. My only comment here is that, Mr. Kehoe, you were talking about a public statement from Registry. Mr. Misetic is talking about a statement from the Prosecution's office. And as for the question of the statement from Prosecution's office, we discussed this extensively at the last Status Conference. The Prosecution did state its position clear that they never made such a statement. I'm not quite sure where we are at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that's incorrect. I don't think they said that the Prosecutor didn't make -- the Prosecutor's spokesman didn't make that statement; and if that's going to be in dispute, we can produce the statements that were made. I think our position prior to the last Status Conference, we also have to make plans and rely reasonably the organs of the Tribunal when they provide us information about when should be prepared to go to trial. We relied in good faith on those organs of the Tribunal. If there's been a change, I think that's fine. But I think what Mr. Kehoe said in his earlier remarks, accelerated trial schedule from the perspective of the Defence, it has been accelerated given the information that we had prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke, Mr. Tieger. Can you tell us what you said to us the last time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here's my understanding of the circumstances just described, and I haven't revisited that for some time. I'll be happy to double-check to make sure what I say to the Court now is accurate, but my understanding is the following: That at some point there was published, in some newspaper or in some forum, a comment by the OTP spokesperson. That comment was a reference to information received from the Registry and an explicit reference information received from the Registry. So what I -- and, of course, I believe I was asked last time whether the -- the OTP had suggested in any way that it was seeking or determining a trial date, and I indicated that, of course, that wasn't the case. I wasn't personally aware of that particular article. I think it was raised, in fact, by Mr. Misetic at that time, similar to the indications he gave the Court today. I checked on that then to see whether it had been some independent assertion by the OTP spokesperson or speculation, and I learned that it was a reference to information provided from the Registry, and that's about all I can tell the Court and would be happy to double-check it if that's useful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess the bottom line is that, in fact, there hasn't been any official scheduling of this trial prior to the current scheduling for the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we go back to the 73 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Judge, but the fact of the reality is that the first notification that we had of a trial in May of 2007 was Your Honour's comments during the last pre-trial hearing. Now, with what we perceive to be an accelerated schedule and the things that have to be done leading up to that, the Rule 72 motions, overall preparing for trial, preparing, going through matters with our client, it has made it extremely difficult to have a meaningful discussion about agreed facts. For instance, Mr. Tieger and I were talking about one particular witness who has a hundred-odd pages of an ECMM report, in addition to three or four statements. There are any number of issues in there that are problematic, could be stipulated to. But taking the time to go through all of that information, interfacing with Mr. Tieger, then talking to General Gotovina, and talking to the Defence counsel for just one witness is a time-consuming endeavour. And, realistically, being able to do all that, yet at the same time prepare for an impending trial, which is now just several months away, is just simply an impossible task. That's not to say that Mr. Tieger and I and the rest of the Defence counsel won't continue to try to do that. But as far as, as we discussed in the last pre-trial with you, Judge, as far as having a meaningful discussion where we go through agreed facts from A to Z in a case of this magnitude, it's impossible on this current time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess the Chamber must understand you to be saying that there would be no agreed facts forthcoming, because it is impossible giving the scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not saying it's -- there will be no agreed facts, Judge. We will do our best to agree on as many facts as we can, but there are logistical difficulties not in seeing our clients but in, of course, talking with each other, talking with Defence counsel, talking with clients, them talking with their clients, to arrive at a general consensus. It's not something that can't happen, Judge. I don't want to tell you that. I'm just telling you it's a time-consuming process; and given where we are in February the 9th of 2007 with a trial in May of 2007 with all of the facts and circumstances to be presented in this case, it's going to be impossible physically to do all that and yet at the same time prepare for trial. I'm not saying that there will be no facts stipulated to, Judge. I am not saying that. But to do a job which we would normally do to take from A to Z, I just have to be perfectly honest with you, Judge, it's physically impossible given the time constraints that we now have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least the record can show that the parties are not only becoming aware of the need for these agreed facts to be submitted today. In the Status Conference in December, this was raised. The parties were aware of this even before the Status Conference of the 5th of December last year that agreed facts are something to be worked on. It's not as if this is something that's new and falling all of a sudden on the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can address -- I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not asking you to address it. I'm just saying, at least, we can put it on the record that that is so. That is fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is a fact, Judge, but I think we also have to note that we didn't have the full breadth of all of the evidence that was coming to us from the Prosecution. I mean, we have had a continuing disclosure. I mean, it's been a daunting task from the Prosecution. This is, please, no criticism from anybody from the Office of the Prosecutor in any way, shape, or form, but the disclosure has ban, in fact, a daunting task for them. So getting involved in stipulated facts before complete disclosures are made is likewise a difficult task, because if, in fact, we attempt to agree to something in large issue that subsequent facts that are revealed to us cause us to change our mind, then we're back at square one. And we, Mr. Misetic and I and all the respective counsel, haven't done the work for our clients the way that we're supposed to. So I understand it's been something that's been on the table, Judge, but it's something that hasn't been -- we have not been able to get into meaningfully until we have everything that needs to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Just maybe to try and round out the problem, the point, is there any indication that can be given as to when these agreed facts can be expected, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From my point of view no, Judge. I gladly turn to my colleague, Mr. Tieger, and see if he has alternate schedule in mind, but I simply don't know at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Prodanovic, do you have any comments to make on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to remind you that in the Cermak, Markac case, before the joinder, we did start stipulating to agreed facts, and we exchanged our original views. However, since the joinder took place and since we did not have a single indictment, we stopped the procedure. So in a way we have already dealt with this. I think it would be best now if the Prosecutor were to come out with his position on this. What would the possible agreed facts be at this point in time. Of course, we will respond in keeping with our own positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prodanovic. Mr. Separovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our position is exactly the same to the position of the Defence teams of General Cermak and General Gotovina. I will not repeat the arguments preferred, but only say that, for instance, 41 witness statements have not been translated into Croatian at all. More than 300 documents remain untranslated at this point. How can we discuss the facts that could possibly be agreed, if we do not have all the material? We need to be precise and accurate in discussing these matters. So I subscribe to the positions of my colleagues, and I state at the same time that we will do our utmost to make progress in this direction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Separovic, thank you for what you ever said. I'm a bit startled by the figures that you are throwing around; 41 statements and 300 documents. We are coming to those items of disclosure and we'll deal with them when we get there, but I thought the picture was slightly different from what you are painting. But be that as it may, that's fine. The Chamber, well, then still encourages the parties to continue to engage on the question of agreed facts and to try and submit the agreed facts as soon as possible before the start of the trial. I guess that's all the Chamber can say at this stage, just to emphasise the fact that the delay in meeting -- in agreeing on the agreed facts is not anticipated at this stage to shift the start date of the trial. Okay. Preliminary motions under Rule 72 would be the next item. Defendant General Ante Gotovina's preliminary motion to dismiss the proposed joinder of the indictment pursuant to Rule 72, filed on 28th of April 2006, was supplemented on the 18th of January this year by his preliminary motion challenging jurisdiction and his motion challenging defects in the form of joinder indictment; and also by General Mladen and General Markac's joint preliminary motion regarding jurisdiction. The Prosecution's responses to all above-three motions was filed on the 1st of February this year, and the Trial Chamber just wanted to inform the parties that a decision would be rendered shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be heard on that issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may be heard, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is an issue that, obviously, we think is substantively crucial prior to even moving into the further preparation of this trial, and I think that an examination of our most recent Rule 72 motions and the grounds for that as well as the challenges to the jurisdiction -- or to the form of the indictment are compelling. The jurisdictional grounds are quite compelling, and we had asked in our brief, and once again I brought it up with Mr. Pittman at the 65 ter conference this morning, if we can ask for oral argument. Mr. Pittman asked us to agree on a date for that oral argument, and I believe with the OTP, with Mr. Tieger, I believe my fellow Defence counsel said that possibly on the week of February 22nd or the date of February 22nd or 23rd, I believe everybody could be present before the Court to argue those motions. I ask the Court for that time because from General Gotovina's perspective and the rest of the Defence, argument on those particular issues are crucial for a proper determination of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is also correct that Defence replies were received yesterday, the 8th of February, on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge. And there was a supplement that we recently filed because there was some mistake on our part with regard to the word count, and I explained -- brought to my attention by Mr. Tieger - no offence - it was a mistake on our part, but nevertheless we did file a reply yesterday to the Prosecutor's position. But I can't urge enough to the Court the need to go through these, I won't say highly technical, but very significant issues vis-a-vis the differences between Hague law and Geneva law and various other matters as it plays into crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I just wanted to clarify one point, Your Honour. We did file a motion for leave to exceed word count this morning, just so the Court is aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any reason to have oral argument on this? Any reason why we couldn't put everything on paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's always -- I found it to be very helpful in a -- in issues such as this to address outstanding questions, and just take a short period of time after Your Honours have been versed on all of the arguments made by the respective defendants and by the OTP, to take some short period of time to clarify any outstanding issues. There are some limitations word wise and space wise that preclude a more extensive discussion about a very, very important issue; and when you examine our briefs regarding the challenges specifically to crimes against humanity you'll see how, I don't want to say complex, but detailed the actual case law is in support of that issue. That being said, Judge, I submit that it would be extremely helpful for the Chamber to take that additional time for oral argument. We can do it into the night of one of those time frames, anything that Your Honours would like, but I would impress upon the Court the need to discuss that in an open forum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There may have been an impression by the mention of the possible dates with -- among the parties that this was a joint request. The Prosecution has not requested oral argument. Obviously, it anticipates that if the Court had deemed it necessary, in light of the original request in the written submission for oral argument, the Court would have indicated to the parties it desired that to happen. The only -- the only thing I would note in addition is that these -- the written submissions have been extensive, and by my calculation the Defence submissions have totaled approximately 17.000 or 18.000 words. I accept fully that any overage was made in good faith and, and I don't raise an issue with that. But that does exceed the word limit of a pre-trial brief, and I think it has been extensively addressed. But I leave it to the Court whether any additional argument is deemed necessary in its view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last issue. If I indicated that -- that Mr. Tieger agreed to oral argument, I didn't mean to indicate that. I my indication was simply on the date that -- if Your Honour was going to -- Your Honours were going to entertain it, that it would appear from consultation with counsel pursuant to Mr. Pittman's instructions that we would come up with this date. I would say with -- finally, with regard to this, Judge, if we are looking into various areas such as reducing the space or reducing the indictment, et cetera, these particular motions will go directly to that and the determination to significantly reduce the indictment that's before us. That's how crucial the legal issues are that are before the Court in these motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is inclined to request maybe a page just giving grounds, written grounds why you need to be heard orally on these issues, because we're not absolutely satisfied with what we have heard this afternoon, and then the Chamber would consider that and come up with its decision after hearing written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Other pending motions relate to the fact that in the last Status Conference, the Defence teams did not object to the Prosecution's combined notice of compliance and motion for protective measures filed on the 19th of October last year. I Guess I'm right there. The Trial Chamber once again informs the parties that a decision will be coming shortly on that point, on that motion. And the other motion pending are also that of General Ivan Cermak and General Mladen Markac's motions for access to confidential testimony in the Martic, Slobodan Milosevic, and Babic cases, as well as Seselj. I imagine the parties are aware this Chamber is not seized of those motions. Those motions are before the respective Chambers that are dealing with those cases, and this Chamber is not in a position to tell the parties when to expect a decision from those various Chambers. Okay? I guess we'll just have to wait for them to respond. Unless anybody has got anything more to say. Mr. Tieger, do you have anything to say on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not at this point, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we have nothing to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Separovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Shall we then move on to the item of disclosure. Now, the state of the disclosure under Rule 66, 68, and 70 should actually be clarified, I think, by you, Mr. Tieger. Apparently Mr. Markac's counsel sent an e-mail to you, I suppose, on the 5th of February, which was copied to the Trial Chamber via the SLO; and in that e-mail, he was requesting a consolidation and streaming lining of the disclosure under the various case numbers. Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect to this issue specifically and the issue somewhat more globally, I don't know how much of an opportunity the SLO had to share with the Bench the discussions at the 65 ter, which were somewhat extensive on this issue and I think somewhat constructive, but if not I'll try to recap those for the Chamber's benefit quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Essentially, we have been in very active and direct contact with the Defence about disclosure matters for some time now. We have put our case management teams together to resolve any -- to identify and resolve any issues. That has been, again, by consensus as acknowledged explicitly at the 65 ter conference, extremely successful. We're continuing to work at that. One of the projects under way is a kind of revamping of the entire disclosure logging process, so we can ensure that, to the extent humanly possible, that every -- that all disclosures have been received and are accessible. With regard to specific problems of the type that the Court mentioned before, we are addressing those directly in the meantime, and that, as I indicated, seems to be as successful an approach as anyone here can envision. And we remain committed to pursuing that approach in an effort to ensure that all existing problems are resolved and all prospective problems are identified and prevented in advance if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, at the last 65 ter conference, the Prosecution had indicated that there were only about eight witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will repeat myself. At the last 65 ter conference, the Prosecution indicated that there were about eight witness statements outstanding; then the Defence indicated that, in fact, there were about 20 translations of such statements outstanding. Now, the number eight and 20, I would have thought, by this time, would have been resolved, whether it was 20 or eight. But, of course, we have heard this of afternoon, the startling figures that have now been raised by Mr. Separovic saying that there are 41 statements and 300 documents that are not still outstanding. Are you able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- clear us on these points?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll do my best, although I may not be able to identify the specific context in which each number arose. What I am aware of is that they referred, on occasion, to different issues. One of the issues that arose was how many statements were translated. Was the -- were there statements that the Defence had that had not yet been translated. Part of that -- part of that was addressed in, as I recall, in a previous 65 ter conference and Status Conference, by noting that not all statements disclosed to the Defence under various Rules would be translated because they were not statements of anticipated witnesses; and then I think the figure eight was, to the best of my recollection, a figure that related to specific identified statements that the parties seemed to agree were statements of witnesses likely to be or intended to be called. Having said that and without going into the details of all that, my current understanding is that with respect to witnesses, who we expect now will be on the Prosecution witness list, that those statements have been translated and disclosed. Now, with respect to the number of documents identified by counsel a few moments ago, I think that's largely embraced by a communication that the Prosecution sent to the Chamber on January 22nd, I believe, in response to an end of the year inquiry from the SLO. And what we indicated then, and what we indicated also at the Status Conference today, was that there were of course any number of, indeed, no doubt a large number of documents disclosed for various reasons that would not necessarily be the subject of translation, because they had not been identified as prospective exhibits or the witnesses had not -- the Prosecution had not made a determination those people should be called. In the communication, I indicated to the Court that there were pending translations, and there would also be additional documents identified as we finalised the exhibit list and finalised the list of witnesses for whom -- for which translations would have to be sought. And I had communicated with the translation services of the institution to determine whether the anticipated documents would present a problem in getting -- it being translated by March 16th; and as I indicated in the communication to the Chamber, I was advised that those documents should be translated. I further indicated that I would keep the Court apprised of any change in that situation if we were advised that that date was in jeopardy and that there would be some documents that would not be translated by -- at the same time we submitted the 65 ter list. And I indicated the same thing at the 65 ter today. I continue to monitor the progress of translations on a very regular basis. My current information is, I think, relatively positive. But as I said in the communication, I will alert the Chamber if the pace is lagging. And I've also taken steps to ensure that if any documents are not translated by that date, that they will receive the highest priority for the translation services. As I know the Court is aware of, because it was raised in previous conferences, the translation resources of the institution are limited, and we were often relegated behind cases that were either in trial or had trial dates pending before this one. And to overcome that, I have been engaged in a regular process of communicating with them, indicating the -- what I had communicated to the Court, and urging them to devote sufficient staff to maximise, to the extent humanly possible, that the documents would be produced by the date I indicated to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the Chamber accept that your short answer is that the time line for disclosure would be March 16th unless otherwise advised by the translations department?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is what I -- that is what I indicated on January 22nd, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you repeat that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm pushing as hard as possible for that to happen, and I will let the Court know if that seems to be -- if something is happening that suggests that that date won't be met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then the Court will then ensure that the time line, as of now, will be March 16th unless you hear otherwise from the translation department. We understand that 68 disclosure is a continuing exercise; but other Rules, 66 and 70, we'll be looking at March 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- unless we hear otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Yes. That's exactly what I tried to indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then again in an e-mail of the 2nd of February this year to the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution indicated that they will provide the 65 ter materials and comprehensive exhibits list electronically on CDs and DVDs and will try to provide an electronic version of the 65 ter list with hyperlinks to the documents. The Prosecution will inform the Trial Chamber in advance if the hyperlink option will not be feasible. I guess the Prosecution asked for confirmation from the Trial Chamber that no master hard copy is needed to be provided to any of the parties but that the electronic set would suffice for 65 ter disclosure. What's your response to that, Mr. Kehoe or Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I -- well, I guess let me speak on all of the disclosure issues that Mr. Tieger has addressed. First, I with agree with him that -- that we have worked diligently on both sides of the aisle to resolve the outstanding issues. They have been significant since our last Status Conference, and there has been good faith on both sides, I think, to resolve those as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But just so you're aware of the status of things, according to our Defence team, again, just for purposes of -- so you know where we are, we're waiting for 30 documents to be disclosed. It's our understanding, and I think Mr. Tieger confirmed it again, the documents which have been provided to us, but which the Prosecution has indicated they do not intend to translate, are documents that will not be used by the Prosecution; and to date, according to our count, there are 477 such documents that far been provided to us. Again, I just want to make that point clear. With respect to this last question of master hard copies, I think that will be sufficient. I -- I qualify that with that one reservation, which is that's assuming that we work out all of these technical issues, which I'm hopeful that we're going to get worked out. On the disclosure, we're anticipating a new disclosure log coming from the Prosecution. The problems, basically, on our side has been that the disclosure log has been very difficult to actually find the documents that are exactly listed on the disclosure log. Assuming that gets worked out, we obviously will be able to find the documents electronically and then go ahead and print them ourselves. But to the extent that if there is a problem and down the line and it becomes simply easier to obtain hard copies of the documents, we may ask that. I don't anticipate that right now, because it's not -- I think it's easier for use to have an electronic form as well, but I just wanted to make sure the Court, given that there are still some outstanding issues, that may be something we explore down the line. But I am hopeful that's going to be resolved in the next two weeks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic. What's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have nothing to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you happy with electronic copies only, without hard copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Separovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The same with us. Electronic copies are fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. From the point of the view of the Bench, if the Bench could be supplied with at least one hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The senior legal officer made that known, and we understand that. Thank you. If I could-- sorry to make any complications in what was about to be a fairly simple issue, but just to clarify two matters. Number one, I think that the electronic disclosures for 65 ter purposes would be independent of the -- it wouldn't be dependent on the disclosure log, so I think documents will be accessible in that disclosure alone. So it's not that the -- and that was the mention of hyperlinks I think. So that's the objective. Maybe that's some assurance. Number two, it's correct that the Prosecution does not intend to translate -- unnecessarily translate documents that won't be exhibits, but that process is ongoing. We're finalising exhibit lists. So the fact that a document has not been translated and is indicated on a current disclosure log currently as untranslated can mean any number of things, including the fact that it's pending translation or the fact that -- that there has been a decision affirmatively made not to use it as an exhibit, or that that decision whether or not it goes in the exhibit list is still awaiting the finalisation of the exhibit list. So I don't -- didn't want counsel to be misled into thinking there hadn't been a misrepresentation that specific documents that hadn't been translated at this point or for which they had not yet received translations will not be on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But to the extent that any of the documents will the not be used for the purposes of the trial, both the Chamber and the Defence would be advised at some time in the near future so they can discard and forget about those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To the extent possible, yes, Your Honour. And perhaps that's one of the virtues of our fairly regular contact, and we will certainly do our -- it certainly will be in the near future, obviously, that filing will be on March 16th. But if we can facilitate that in the interim, we're happy to do so and if we can find a way to indicate certain documents that the Defence need not concern themselves with, we'll try to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The Bench appreciates and notes the virtues of regular contact and encourages that contact to be maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My proposal is that we work this out amongst ourselves. I know that we have a long agenda still to, but I want to make sure the record is clear. Our position -- our understanding is somewhat different than that, and the reason is that the disclosure log actually states that a translation is pending for documents that are currently in the process of being translated. We did have discussions about this issue at both of the last Status Conferences, where my other colleagues raised the fact that they could not read documents because they hadn't been translated. And I believe that it was represented that if we haven't asked for a translation, you can rely on the fact that we don't intend to use the document. Rather than take it -- more of the Court's time, my proposal is that Mr. Tieger and I and the rest of the counsel try to work this out ourselves, so we don't take up more time of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Misetic, and the Court indulges that. Would you please make sure that you sort that out amongst yourselves as quickly as you possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The other point was that the Prosecution indicated at the last Status Conference that it was awaiting approval and Rule 70 from the provider of certain documents, approximately a hundred of them, before it could disclose them to the Gotovina defence and the other Defences. Has this approval been given by now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This has been a continuing matter, which is why these particular Rule 70 documents have arisen on a number of Status Conferences and 65 ters. That's not to say that they're the only Rule 70 documents with which the OTP must deal and for which it must seek permission, but somehow these were identified quite some time ago. And there was some focus on them and that the pending permission has not yet occur. I will say that the provider was gracious enough to contact us recently as of two days ago, in fact, to let us know that they're continuing their review and that the matter remains in process. That was another matter, I may add, that I addressed in the response to the end of the year update from the senior legal officer, and I indicated at that time that we had taken some extraordinary steps in an effort to facilitate this and had been advised by the provider's representative that we had done everything possible at that time, even beyond that. After we received the Scheduling Order from the Court, I contacted the provider and let them know what the new deadlines were in an effort to encourage an expedited review. And as I say, the most recent communication is the one I indicated to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the communication you've just received recently from the provider, is there any indication of a time line by when they think they can provide this information, this permission?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there is not. All I can say is that -- as I mentioned, that they are aware of our time line, and perhaps it's encouraging that they did not indicate in this communication that that would be in jeopardy. And I -- in fact, I will contact them again and do my best to determine whether there is a projected completion of review date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will appreciate that very much. Thank you so much. I don't imagine that any of the Defence counsel have anything to say or let me not preempt. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Separovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll then move on to the next point. General Gotovina's Defence counsel had asked for instructions in an e-mail to the senior legal officer on the 5th of February this year on how to interpret the Trial Chamber's 14 July 2006 non-disclosure order, particularly on whether the Defence is allowed to disclose previous witness statements provided to the Prosecution, to the witnesses themselves, and to their governments. The Trial Chamber finds the question redundant since the referred order clearly states what should be done. Moreover, the Trial Chamber is a little surprised that it has been asked ex parte and confidentially not to disclose the specifics of the matter to the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber has since been advised that this morning the matter was ventilated openly between the parties. Now, the Prosecution is aware of the Defence's intentions to approach some of the witnesses who might be Prosecution witnesses. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the Prosecution has always been aware of our intention to approach Prosecution witnesses. That issue was specifically litigated at length last year with the Trial Chamber, with the Trial Chamber concluding in the 14 July order that there is nothing precluding the Defence from contacting Prosecution witness, with the provision that the Prosecution had 14 days from that order with respect to any witnesses they have disclosed to us to seek protective measures for those witnesses under Rule 75, which would then require some sort of methodology whereby we could contact those protected witnesses under Rule 75 through the Prosecution. Subsequent to that, in September, the Prosecution filed a request for such measures with respect to I believe six witnesses. The Defence did not object, and that motion is still pending before the Chamber with respect to those six witnesses only. With respect to every other witness that the Prosecution has disclosed to the Defence, the 14 July order makes clear that we can go ahead and contact them. So the purpose of the ex parte or confidential nature of the request wasn't to contact witnesses that we shouldn't be contacting; but rather in order to protect work product of the Defence in terms of who specifically we're contacting and why, that that issue be addressed because the parties obviously have a right to prepare their own cases in accordance with Rule 70 and to protect their work product. That was the only intention. Otherwise, it's our understanding pursuant to the July 14 order that we have the right to contact Prosecution witnesses, except for those that are currently pending before the Chamber, those six witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the explanation. At least that's -- what caused us surprise was the fact that it was confidential and ex parte to the Chamber. But now given your explanation, it's even more surprising that the request for interpretation has been asked at all, if this matter has been litigated and ventilated in court and decided finally. But no need to go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, we're just trying to do the right thing. We were trying not to contravene any order, and people were asking us for this. Governments were asking me in particular for this; and, candidly, Judge, I was trying to cross the T's and dot the I's and not do anything improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for the crossing and the dotting. Specifically, Mr. Tieger, this progress on the Rule 68 disclosures. I know it's a continuing exercise, but we want to know what progress has been made in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's a little hard to identify the progression of an endless exercise, but we -- I mean, part of that process involves going through materials that are not accessible to the Defence. And we have been concentrating on that to ensure that we get through it as early as possible. The -- I will confess to the Court, I did not check the status of that progress immediately before this conference. But the last time I did, which was not long ago, it seemed like we were reasonably on target for ensuring that we had been through that material well in advance of the commencement of trial. But in light of the Court's question and my response, it's -- I think it would be prudent if I went back and double checked to see exactly the pace of our progress through those materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the Chamber does appreciate that it's an endless exercise. However, the Rule does say to the extent that the Prosecution knows of such material. So at least to that extent, it is not an endless exercise. And that's only the reason we asked the question, to the extent that you know of the existence of any such material, how far are you in disclosing that which you know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we're quite current, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're quite current.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we have processes in place to ensure that those documents are disclosed as -- as soon as practicable, and I think we've been successful at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give a time line on as soon as practicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's only -- it's only a matter of logistics. We bring them to the attention of the those persons responsible for collecting them and sending them; and within a relatively short period of their, meaning what, a week, two weeks at most, of their identification, we ensure that they're sent out, barring some logistical problem or emergency that interferes with that. In other words, if we could humanly do it, if I read a document and it came within my actual knowledge that it was Rule 68, I'd hand it right over the bar table to counsel; and to the extent we can do that given our distances, we attempt to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The next one - again, I'm sorry I'm coming back to you again, Mr. Tieger - comprehensive 92 bis, 92 ter protective measures motions. Any progress in that direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We had a discussion about that at the 65 ter. Prosecution was asked by the senior legal officer to identify some date between the submission of the pre-trial brief and witness list and exhibit list and the submission of the Defence pre-trial brief that would be suitable for the submission of 92 bis motions. And I indicated that we would look at that as soon as possible and provide some feedback to the Court in that regard. So I haven't -- we haven't had an opportunity to act on that yet, but my understanding is that essentially the Prosecution has been asked to identify some date between that time when -- when that can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the Prosecution will indicate that date?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. We'll get back to the -- we'll do our best to get back to the Court sometime at the beginning of next week or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any comment on that point from the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, just as an overarching kind of question, the Trial Chamber would be interested to find out when it can expect disclosure to be concluded. Now, just as a general -- is it possible to give us this answer, say by the 20th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I understand the Court correctly, I think it would be possible to give the Court an answer by -- well, the 20th of March. I think -- Your Honour, is that -- I need some clarification. You'd like us to get back to the Chamber in writing by a certain date as to when disclosure would be completed in its entirety, other than Rule 68 obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Barring Rule 68, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if I may, Your Honour. Unless the Court needs a specific date here at the moment, I would be more comfortable, and I think I'd be acting more appropriately if the Court gave me an opportunity to consult with my team and make sure that I'm not overlooking some -- some problems and not committing us to a date that -- that generates difficulties that I'm not thinking of at the moment. So if you wouldn't mind, I'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. And when you have consulted with your team, would you be kind enough to relate to the SLO the date that you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, I'd be pleased to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. At this stage, the Chamber just wants to reiterate the time lines as envisaged up to the commencement of the trial pursuant to the Scheduling Order of 17th January. The Prosecution is expected to file its submissions pursuant to Rule 65 ter (E) by Friday the 16th of March, and a Status Conference is to take place on Tuesday, the 3rd of April, beginning at 2.30 in the afternoon in a courtroom to be advised. And the Defence is to file their submissions pursuant to Rule 65 ter (F) by Thursday, the 5th of April. The Pre-Trial Conference pursuant to Rule 73 bis is to take place on Friday, the 27th of April. Opening statements by the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 84 is to take place on Monday, the 7th of May. And an opening statement by the Defence, if any at this stage, is to take place on the 8th of May, and evidence will be presented starting 9th of May. Okay. I guess all those time lines are in the Scheduling Order, but the Chamber just wanted to reiterate them to the parties. The next item will be the potential conflicts of interest between the various Defence teams. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that we're in --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court will adjourn for 20 minutes and come back at five to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I pick up with you, Mr. Separovic now. Before we went to the break, you sounded in a hurry to get a decision whether or not you should stay in this trial. It looks like in fact the decision in the first place should be your decision and not anybody else's. So to the extent that you are being delayed, it looks like you have nobody but Mr. Separovic to look to. Would I be right in surmising that? We have the -- the opinion of the ADC. I'm sure you have read it, and it's for you to decide how you're going to conduct yourself based on that opinion. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will reiterate what I said in closed session before. There is nothing that I can say in private session that I cannot say in public. That's one thing. Second, I assert that I am not in a conflict of interest, that I am not a necessary witness, and that's why I am ready with my colleague Mr. Mikulicic, who will speak with your leave on legal issues and legal standards, to speak on facts. Third, if I were to leave two and a half months before the beginning of trial, General Markac would be irreparably prejudice because he would no longer be on an equal footing with other Defence teams or the Prosecution team, because a new Defence counsel cannot get sufficiently prepared in two and a half months. As I said, I do not believe I am in a conflict of interest, but let me explain once again why I am looking forward to an early decision. The Trial Chamber is the one to decide. It is not my decision. Weighing all the arguments for and against, the Trial Chamber has to decide in order to avoid a situation in which I could be accused of contempt of court or of violating our code of conduct, our professional code of conduct. It is my position, therefore, that I am not a necessary witness, that I do not have a conflict of interest, and that General Markac would be irreparably prejudiced were I to leave at this point. But I believe that it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide. I hope that you will allow me and Mr. Mikulicic to further explain our position, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't you want to explain your position to the full before you sit down?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to explain why I believe I do not have a conflict of interest to substantiate my position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether at this point in time the Chamber is trying to determine whether you are or you are not in -- in a conflict of interest. The Chamber is presented with an opinion from the ADC, which makes certain findings about your position in particular, and we -- that's why I said to you a little earlier when you came back that based on that position by the -- of the opinion, the decision is actually yours. And I hear you keep saying you want a decision from the Bench, but I don't think we are at that stage yet. I thought -- I think we are at a stage where you've got to indicate what you intend to do given the opinion, without giving motivation for it. Are you carrying on or are you not carrying on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think we have understood each other. My answer is yes, I wish to continue, and I'm going to continue all the way until a decision is made by this Trial Chamber to make me leave if the Trial Chamber chooses to make such a decision. I can present further arguments, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think that it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Separovic, a few questions. First, on the matter itself. Let's just assume that there would be any dispute about who would have been responsible, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Defence, high-ranking military -- high-ranking officers about what crimes that were there to be investigated and to -- and to be prosecuted. If you, as a witness, would have to testify on these kind of matters, do you see that there is a -- that you might be in a dilemma when you would say, "No, it was mainly the Ministry of Justice," then you would perhaps take some blame for things that have happened. If you with say, "No, it was the Minister of Defence," or you'd say,"It was the high-ranking officers," do you understand that your own position is involved when testifying on these issues if you would be called as a witness in the cases against the three accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'm aware of that. But you must take into account my assertion and my belief that the matters that I could be asked to speak about could easily be the subject of testimony of another ten very competent people. If the question is whether somebody's culpable or not, I cannot speak to that. Therefore, such a situation could not arise in my opinion. As to how the justice system functioned, there are any number of very competent witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Separovic, let's just assume that the Chamber would consider the former Minister of Justice, the first one, the highest responsible for perhaps what happened in the Ministry of Justice to testify on these matters and not the 13 other witnesses you're suggesting. What then? The Prosecution perhaps plan to have you as one of the prominent persons, because I do understand that you -- there's no dispute about you being a former Minister of Justice of Croatia. Is that -- okay. Let's just assume that the Prosecution would consider you to be the best witness or the Chamber or any of the other counsel. What then?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but that's a hypothetical question. You're asking me to respond to something that might, but also might not happen. If the Prosecutor deemed that this was a potential subject of contention, they could have let us know much earlier. Why would this issue become suddenly a matter of dispute two and a half months before the start of trial? Maybe the purpose is to delay the trial, to put a new problem before the Defence, but if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Separovic, that's not what I asked you. I didn't ask you to comment on what the possible consequences are because that's clear enough. Then may I ask you one other question, perhaps put something to you and see whether you would agree or disagree with that. You say the Trial Chamber should decide. You may have noticed that from the words of Judge Moloto that he considers it's the first duty of counsel to consider the matter and to see whether he has to take a decision. Now, you have alluded to the possibility that this Trial Chamber would take a decision. The Chamber has discussed the matter; and on the basis of the documents we received, there's still another possibility, and that is that the Executive Council of the ADC would take a decision, and from what I understand not primarily if you withdraw but especially if you would, as we now understand you're not intending to, if you would not withdraw, which might have quite drastic consequences not only for this case but also for your -- for your position as a Defence counsel in this Tribunal, because you know that membership of the ADC is one of the requirements for Defence counsel to act before this Tribunal. That's part of a scenario I did not hear any comment on from your side. Could you -- could you tell me whether what you think the role of the ADC in this respect would be, especially after in the advisory opinion it is established -- at least it's said that there are good reasons to believe that there is already a conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what is most important to me are the interests of my client. No other interests come close. Therefore, I hold that the findings of the ADC are of advisory nature. It is possible that my bar association, having heard legal arguments and having studied the precedents decided upon by this court and precedents from common law which they may not have been aware of earlier, will change their opinion. But I would appreciate it if these precedents be taken account and my bar association decides whether it would be possible to conduct a vetting process, a verification process to establish whether other witnesses could be called to provide the testimony on matters that I would be asked to testify to, and the bar association should hear about such precedents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was -- as a matter of fact, I was referring to the ADC, which is a bar association as well and which decides on membership of its members. So apart from that, I'm a little bit surprised that you would leave it to the, I then take it, the Croatian Bar Association to see whether or not this Chamber should call other witnesses rather than -- whether there would be a possibility for that. But let's not focus on that. But especially your position within the ADC --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be a misunderstanding. I'm sorry. It is a misunderstanding. I'm sorry. With your leave, when I spoke about the bar association, I meant the ADC, and I meant exclusively the ADC. They are the only bar association that I regard as mine. I thought perhaps they could hear my arguments and maybe change their opinion. If they want to exclude me, to make me withdraw, maybe they could organise an adversarial hearing and a decision could be made on that basis. So far they have only provided findings of advisory nature. I would appreciate it if you would allow me and give me the possibility of entering into a discussion, a polemic with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Would you agree with me that if there's an apparent risk of -- even if you would take it that at this moment there's no conflict of interest, that if there is an apparent risk, there would be one in the future that would be a reason to withdraw as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I do not believe that is the case. I don't think we should go that far in our interpretation and say that there is that possibility, because then we could easily argue there is a possibility of abusing that situation to make me withdraw at a certain stage of the proceedings once they start. That is why my position is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for Mr. Separovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Separovic. If I may address a question to Mr. Karnavas. You've heard what Mr. Separovic said. The advisory opinion is quite clear on his situation, and the Displinary Committee of the ADC decided not to act at this stage, but to defer to the Executive Council because the Executive Council had asked for the opinion. What would be the normal next course of action within the ADC given the answer that we have just got?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, let me say that the ADC, as a professional association, finds these sorts of issues extremely serious. We are an association to protect the interest of the Defence lawyers but, more importantly, to make sure that the rights of the accused whom we represent are fully protected. So we -- we bear every decision we make in mind with the rights of the accused. Now, I was struck by one of the questions that was asked by you, Mr. President, and that was that you had expected the Defence lawyer to have acted on his own -- on his own accord given the decision that was rendered by the ADC. As a policy matter, the ADC expected the same of its members upon receipt of such an advisory opinion. The Executive Committee saw this. Obviously, it felt extremely comfortable with the content of the decision. I think it's a very detailed decision, the situation is rather serious, and that's why I brought Mr. Murphy with me, who is the chair of the disciplinary council. So when this issue came to us, the Executive Committee, we passed it along to the Registrar. We did not act at that point in time thinking that perhaps counsel, because this decision affects more than just the one of the Defence teams, would act on their own accord. I don't believe it's a matter of us misunderstanding the continental system versus the common law system. That's not an issue. We do understand the jurisprudence. We do have rules, and this is a party-driven system. And I think that the one question asked by Judge Orie is very pointed, what if, what if the Trial Chamber on its own wished to call a particular witness on its own, which it is it entitled to do, and that may in this case may be lead counsel, and that poses a grave issue. So, what would the ADC do? Well, frankly, we believe the Trial Chamber should act primarily because the ADC does not want to usurp from the Trial Chamber its authority. For instance, what if ADC were to take measures and say, "You must withdraw," and then the Trial Chamber for other reasons decided that the ADC's decision lacked merit and then overruled the ADC? If, on the other hand, from what I'm hearing, today the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the decision itself should stand, albeit as advisory, then obviously the ADC would have to make a formal request at least to -- to the counsel involved in this case to take the appropriate actions necessary as indicated in the opinion. But, again, what we're concerned primarily is not getting caught in the middle, where we, based on an advisory opinion, take a position, then we're overruled by the Registry or the Trial Chamber. We do keep in mind that the Trial Chamber has set a trial date that, that we don't want to interrupt the proceedings. The ultimate call is up to the Trial Chamber, we believe. But, obviously, if the Trial Chamber were to indicate that this decision stands and it has merit, then, obviously, the ADC would have to take appropriate measures such as requesting, perhaps, the gentleman to strongly consider withdrawing or else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say the ultimate decision lies with the Trial Chamber. Wouldn't you say the intermediate decision lies with the ADC?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've been watching this Status Conference, and you seem to be hitting the head of the nail on each of your questions. Yes, you're quite right, Mr. President. You're quite right. But, again, from a policy position, what we're concerned is being seen as trying to drive a counsel out of a case only to be overruled later on by a Trial Chamber, and that puts us in a very difficult position. But I take your point, I understood your question, and the short answer is, yes. We're the step in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you say if the decision of the ADC would be overruled by the Trial Chamber, where do you find the competence of the Trial Chamber to overrule decisions on membership issues in the ADC?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this is a -- as I understand, this is -- they're coming in under Rule 44. What we're -- it's one thing for us to strike someone from the list, for instance, or to say they are no longer in compliance, in compliance with the ADC. But nonetheless the Trial Chamber decides because they set a trial date that they want this case to go forward, and the Trial Chamber could very well say, "Well, albeit we have this advisory opinion, we find that it lacks merit, that perhaps they've reached the wrong conclusion," in which case the Trial Chamber decides irrespective of ADC to keep counsel in the case and overrule the decision of the -- of the ADC. That's our concern. We're being placed in the middle. And that's why when we transferred the matter to the -- to the Registry, we then expect the Registry to take appropriate action. I hope I've answered your question. We are in a delicate position that we don't have quite the enforcement powers that some folks think we have or should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you understand, Mr. Karnavas, that the Trial Chamber usually would act upon the complaint of somebody or upon a situation arising and being there virtually in the face of everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, therefore, to suggest that you are being caught in the middle is really to pass the buck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, you seem to be hitting it on the head. I'm not trying to quite the buck. I'm trying to navigate through some difficult channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed trying to navigate yourself out it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I take your point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Certainly, the Trial Chamber can't be seized of it before it is brought before it as an issue. This issue arose simply because in a joint application, somebody indicated he might call Mr. Separovic, the matter went on appeal, the appeal court said it hasn't arisen yet. It may arise if this happens. However, the advisory opinion says it has arisen, and it is for the ADC, therefore, to decide if it has arisen. Within its own rules and codes, is there a course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which would not necessarily be a course of action just yet before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. Perhaps because I'm more familiar with my own jurisdiction, normally the Court would have stretched in. But, again -- again, in my jurisdiction if there was a conflict of interest to arise that was not brought to the Court's attention by the attorney, the attorney would be sanctioned. So I come from a different culture where it's -- the attorney would have to be pro-active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But understand, Mr. Karnavas, for now it seems to me as if the conflict for purposes of the Chamber to act would arise the moment Mr. Separovic was called as a witness and he took the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It does seem as if within the rules of the ADC in terms of the advisory opinion, you don't have to wait until that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. I think -- I think the opinion is rather clear, Mr. President, in my opinion. And Mr. Murphy is here to address that in a more thorough fashion. But as I read the opinion, and it's rather clear, I think you would be imprudent to wait and see whether that occasion would arise, I think. Because as you have indicated, in essence it has arisen already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if this Court -- for this Court to be seized of the matter, there ought to be -- there should be some kind of complaint put before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we -- we assumed and perhaps wrongly that the advisory opinion was in essence a vehicle for which the Trial Chamber could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that could be as well. I trust, Mr. President -- I trust -- I'm not trying to avoid answering directly, but I'm just trying to, as I've indicated, finesse the situation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you have told us what you can tell us about Mr. Separovic, and I understand that about Mr. Prodanovic the opinion does say that the conflict has not arisen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there anything you would like to say on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
