utterances.text: I would prefer to have Mr. Murphy address it, but again I think if you read the -- the advisory opinion is rather clear, in my -- in my opinion, in that I don't think -- well, attorney -- counsel always has to -- they know their case better than anyone else, and of course they have to exercise certain -- certain judgement, professional judgement. And I think the opinion does seem to indicate that at some point for all intents and purposes it will arise. At least that's how I read it, or there's a very high probability that it will arise. And in that case, then it begs the question at what point should you act. In my professional opinion, you act as soon as you become aware that the possibility exists that it might arise, as opposed to waiting for the situation to actually come to that point. But then, again, I don't want to go into the merits. Mr. Murphy is much more prepared to answer that question, and I would welcome his input.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Murphy, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly. I should say, first of all, because there may have been a certain misunderstanding about what an advisory opinion is and what its effect is, the disciplinary council of the ADC has very, very limited powers. We -- we cannot act in any way until we are asked to do so by either a member of the association or in this case by the Executive Committee. This matter began because in November Mr. Karnavas, on behalf of the Executive Committee asked us for an advisory opinion. But as Mr. Separovic said, the advisory opinion is exactly that. It is simply a statement of our legal position under the code of conduct,; and before we could -- before the disciplinary council could take any further action, some further request would have to be made to us. Perhaps, for example, a member would make a formal complaint. Now, if that happened, under our constitution, there is quite an elaborate procedure, as Your Honour can imagine, with a certain due process for the member of the bar concerned. And, frankly, it would not be feasible to conclude such a proceeding before the trial date was -- was set, which has been set in this case, arrived. It just wouldn't happen. So from our position in the Displinary Committee or council, Your Honour, the last thing we would want to do would be to disrupt the -- the holding of the trial and make it more difficult for the accused, and so I think that in a practical sense our, hands are -- or somewhat tied here. And when Your Honour said that it was primarily a matter for the individual counsel to decide, I found myself noting in agreement with that, because I think from a practical point of view that is really the situation here, that each of these counsel has to decide what to do. Whether at a later time in certain eventualities, if they should arise during the trial, whether other action might be needed at that point, it probably would come from the Trial Chamber because you'd be faced with a practical difficulty that it had arisen during trial and then that it would have to be solved. I will say this if I may, Your Honour, one other thing. As far as the advisory opinion itself is concerned. Your Honours have obviously read it, and you will appreciate for the most part it tracks the observations made by the Appeals Chamber in -- when the matter went up on the joinder question. And we were very scrupulous to -- to observe the findings of the Appeals Chamber, and I think the only addition that we made to what the Appeals Chamber said was -- they were obviously not concerned with the precise terms of the code of conduct. It wasn't before the Appeals Chamber. It was before us. So we had to interpret what Article 14 of the code of conduct meant; and as Your Honour knows, we took the view that it imposed a certain positive duty on counsel. But other than that, I think Your Honour will had find that really everything that we've said was said by the Appeals Chamber on the 25th of October. And so to that extent, we do have a finding -- findings in the record already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Murphy. I guess we have heard -- I guess we have heard had the parties, counsel on the matter. We haven't got much time. We still have another major item to deal with. The Chamber cannot make a decision on the point right now -- sorry. Yes, Mr. Separovic. Yes, sir, would you like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please. Just five minutes of patience for allowing my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, to speak of the legal nature of the matter involved and jurisprudence. This will cast a completely different light on what the ADC has said. Please do allow us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Separovic, we have very tight time constraints. Do you think it can -- can we get the submissions in writing by counsel in about three days? Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, we can do it in writing, but we really don't need more than five minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But we need the time left for the other issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, in writing then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am aware that other counsel have sort of been quiet. I guess you are still quiet, Mr. Kehoe, on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly. The Court did talk about the -- with Mr. Karnavas about the intermediate step. I would just simply note the jurisprudence of the Tribunal makes it incumbent on the Trial Chamber to act in the face of foreseeable risks that threaten to will disrupt the proceedings or threaten its integrity. And I noted, as Mr. Murphy did, that the holding or findings of the Appeals Chamber indeed tracked the language and the findings of the advisory opinion found at page 19 of the Appeals Chamber indicating that they found such conflict to exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest also to you, Mr. Prodanovic, in case you have anything to say, please to submit it in writing, if you have anything to say still on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, we shall avail ourselves of that opportunity to express our views in writing. However, since you have put this question in general, it pertains to us as well. How an attorney should act if his disciplinary council establishes that there is potential conflict of interest. That question is very clear to us; then one should leave the said defence if there is agreement on that. However, we think that that opinion is based on unfamiliarity with the facts in the case involved. Oh, please let me. Just a few words, and I'll elaborate on the rest in writing. And, basically, what is important is to see how the potential conflict of interest will be resolved, and that will be -- and that is actually due to unfamiliarity with facts. I would like to indicate the clear distinction that exists from the ruling of the Appeals Chamber from the 25th of October that says there is a possible future conflict of interest, but also what is indicated are the ways that it can be resolved or overcome. Guided by the views of the Trial Chamber, we gave our own statements -- rather, the statements of Mr. Ademi, who is a witness in this case and an accused in a completely different case concerning a matter that took place two years before this. So I'm not even going to refer to that now. So there is a difference in terms of how this conflict of interest could be resolved between the disciplinary council and the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic, you're going a little longer than I thought you were going to take. Do you mind if I cut you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you have any further submissions, may I suggest that you put them in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very gladly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do suggest to everybody, anybody who still wants to make any further submissions in writing, please do so within the next three days, by Wednesday next week, in other words. I'll give you three working days. Thank you very much. We'll close this matter at that point. The next item on the agenda may or may not -- the rest of the people may or may not want to stay for it, and if they so wish they would be excused; but if they wish to say, they're welcome to stay. This is the matter relating to the compliance with the provisional release conditions. Those of you who would like to be excused are excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with all due respect, if we could be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You excused Mr. Kehoe and Mr. Misetic. Thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Murphy. The Chamber wants to thank you, specifically, Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Murphy for you time. I don't know whether there is any transport arrangement for General Gotovina. But if he does want to leave, he's also excused if there is separate transport for him arranged. I don't know about that pat, but he's not forced to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We want to take an opportunity to chat with the general in back if we can. If possible, he can go in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The transcript cannot reflect what counsel is saying. No microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to take the opportunity. I think they probably all will be going back together, but we were just going to take a few minutes to chat with the general before the other hearing ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not able to -- to say yea or nay on that one. I think you've got to sort it out with the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I just forgot to say, Mr. Markac also may be excused if -- there is an order that has just been filed reinstating General Markac's provisional release. Do you hear that, Mr. Separovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Your Honour, I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just saying there is a decision filed reinstating Mr. Markac's provisional release with effect from, I think, tomorrow. Okay? Thank you very much. So he's also --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- also allowed to leave if he so wishes. He can wait outside, unless he wants to listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shall we just take a short break for the security to escort the people out. We will come back just now. Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 6.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic, the Chamber would like to find out from you whether we should go into private session, or even from anybody else, from the Prosecution. What prompts this question is simply because you made a filing confidentially, and we just want to find out whether we should go into private session to discuss this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well then. We'll then stay in open session, and I'll ask Judge Orie to lead us in the discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to put a few questions both to counsel, but also to Mr. Cermak himself. Now, he's quite at a distance, but we'll try to see whether it -- we can work at this distance, Mr. Cermak, or whether we -- I would perhaps later invite you to sit here if necessary. I'd like to clarify a few factual matters, which I learned from the submissions made. You are aware that we are talking about three events: One lunch on the 29th of December; the New Years Eve party, 31st of December; and a happening on the 4th of January of this year, that is a ski race where at least it was suggested that you might have violated the conditions of your provisional release. First question. I don't know whether I have to address you, Mr. Cermak, or whether I have to address your counsel. It appears from the submissions that any activity that was business related would be allowed under the conditions of the provisional release. Is that the position of the Defence? And Defence is Defence counsel and accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then take you -- do you remember what the exact conditions were that were put to Mr. Cermak? Could you tell us where you find that whatever business event there is that Mr. Cermak was allowed to attend. Where do we find that? I mean, could you -- what were the terms? What were the conditions? How were they phrased?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conditions from the annex to the decision; that was that he could go to work in Zagreb between 7.00 a.m. and 7.00 p.m. on workdays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on workdays. He could go to his business premises, yes. And would that mean that you could go to a restaurant as well, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was our interpretation of it. That is a bit of an extensive interpretation. But if I may say so, he hardly ever went to Zagreb because, basically, he moved his business premises already, on the basis of the first decision to Krapinske Toplice where he resides. And the fact that in this case -- oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you at this moment. I would like to put a few questions to you. You said he already moved his business to Krapinske Toplice, but nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But nevertheless he asked, he requested that he would go to his business in Zagreb. You said there was -- there was hardly any need to do so, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, not really. That's not what I said. It's not that there was no need to go, but he went rarely. Could you please have a look at what it was that I actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, he was allowed to leave the confines of his residence in Krapinske Toplice and travel to and from the seat of the company, which is a certain address in Zagreb, Marticeva 65. Is it your interpretation that travelling from the exact address where you live and to the business premises would allow you to go whatever business place in between?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what we thought. But, obviously, on the basis of your questions, we thought wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, I put a next question perhaps, Mr. Cermak, to you yourself. You attended a birthday lunch on the 29th of -- a lunch at the occasion of a birthday of a business partner in Zagreb. Could you tell us what was the distance between the restaurant and your -- the business premises where you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just stopped by at this birthday party of my business partner after leaving work. That was around 2.00. Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you the distance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distance is perhaps a thousand metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know if you have seen, but a picture was published at that lunch where you are seated at a table. Have you seen that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've seen that picture. I just came to wish him happy birthday. We had a drink, and my wife and I went home. And all the rest-- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that comes next the question. Someone is standing in that picture and a woman is sitting next to you. Is that your wife or --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my wife, yes. She was at the birthday party, at my friend's birthday party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, my next question would be about the New Year's Eve. In the submissions, it was said that this was outside business hours. Could you tell us from what time to what time until what time did you attend this New Years Eve party?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I attended the New Year's Eve party - well, since you're asking me about the time - from 9.00 in the evening until 1.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Then you said it was outside business hours. What was the day of this New Year's Eve party? Was it a working day? Was it a weekend day?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] New Year was during the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the conditions clearly state that you're not allowed, as it says, "but not on Saturdays or Sundays." Could you tell us why you considered it to be acceptable to go to Zagreb outside business hours on a day which was specifically excluded from the privilege given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can I tell you? I've made a mistake, Your Honour. It was lack of caution on my part, but I felt it was necessary to see my friends and business partners. Some of them came from abroad, and knowing that I would be going to The Hague soon, and also it had to do with work. I employ about 600 people by the way, so I am responsible for their existence and my own; and, quite simply, I felt the need to see these people. And it wasn't my intention -- it was not my intention to bring into question the decisions of the Tribunal or the Tribunal itself in any way. With your permission, I would like to say a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few more questions for you, before I give you an opportunity to. The third event was the ski race. Now, I have seen the submissions by counsel and the submissions by the government of Croatia. There are a few things that are slightly different in the one or in the other. Mr. Cermak, one of the things that -- in which there's a slight difference in the submissions made by the government - I don't know whether it is a difference - but you say that the slopes on which the events were held are on the Hrvatsko Zagorije side and lie several kilometres from your house; whereas, the government says since the event was in the vicinity of his registered residence, a little more than five kilometres away from his house. Now, I see "a little more than five kilometres," and I see "several kilometres." What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More than five kilometres. From the side of Zagorije, on the side closer to my house, to my residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much kilometres would it be by car?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the start of the path in Bistra, it would be around ten, a little over ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking about the place where you were, Sljeme, as far as I understand, where you, as I understand, picked up your son and your wife. To your house, how much would that be by car?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I went to Zagreb on business, I had agreed with my wife that I should take her and my son and go together with them to the Zagorije house. We often go via Sljeme because it's much less jammed, much less crowded. I just wanted to make it clearer to you and to respond to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please respond to my questions first. My question was just what is the distance between Sljeme and your house, if you go by car.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Sljeme to my house by car, it's around 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite you to come sit here next to the ELMO and then we can have a look at it. Could that be put on the ELMO. Yes. Mr. Cermak, I have consulted some information in the public domain, and I found a map, a map with a scale on it, and I reproduced that scale on this map. Is that -- and I tried to draw a line between what is indicated as Sljeme in approximately what I, on the basis of the documents, considered to be the direction of your house; and as the crow flies, could you perhaps, first, at the ELMO point at where your house is? If you take a pen so that we all can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As the crow flies, well beyond 20 kilometres on the scale of this map, which would mean that by road, it would certainly take far more, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when you ask me about the distance of my house from Sljeme, I said 15 kilometres. I didn't mean the top of Sljeme. I meant the edge of those slopes around Sljeme. Because Stubicke Toplice is the exact beginning of the slopes of Sljeme. I went to Sljeme because that's the road to Zagreb. When I reached the slopes of Sljeme from Krapinske Toplice and another Toplice, that's exactly where the slope of Sljeme begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Now, could you point for us exactly where the spectators to the ski event were. Where would we find the place where the people would view the event.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult to show this on this map because it has no contour lines, but the ski pat of Sljeme faces Zagreb and faces Krapinske Toplice. It's all within my district, my neighbourhood. Whether it's here or here, I'm not sure. But the path faces exactly this side. Stubicke Toplice is where the path begins, and it faces Sljeme. It's not on the Zagreb side. It's on the Zagorije side, and the path is visible from the entire Zagorije.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said you -- and I see a also slight difference between the submissions made by counsel and the submissions made by the government. Your counsel says you often took this road in order to avoid traffic jams; whereas, the government says you often used this road in order to avoid traffic jams, and that's what you did on that day as well. Is that -- which is the two is the correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout these two years, I very rarely went to Zagreb because I had moved most of my business to Krapinske Toplice, and it was only occasionally that I used this road. It's one of the options -- one of the possible roads going to Zagreb where I can go to my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to correct. You said. You said "occasionally." Now was it that day that you wanted to avoid the traffic jam as well, that that's why you took that road?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was because my son and wife were skiing. My 10 year old child skis rather seriously. That's the only ski event that actually takes place in Croatia. And for the love of my child, whom I have never been able to take there ever since this story in The Hague started, I did it because I had been promising and promising that. The child really adores that sport. I really did not believe, Your Honour, because I have been cooperating with this institution for so many years --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have no opportunity to take him with you in previous years or --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the earlier years, I was unable to take him skiing because this ski complex was just completed two years ago. It's the first time Zagreb and Croatia produced a ski complex that is able to -- to cater to such an event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which leaves it possible that you would have taken him there the year before, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the earlier years, he went to ski with an instructor. He had his own instructor, and he skied on that pist [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the year before that same event. Did you take him then or did you go there at all the year before?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the same event, yes. The same competition we attended last year. We took him to just watch. It was until 5.00 that the first round -- the first run lasted, and right after that we went home. But I did not think of it as a violation because it's within my district, the area where I am allowed to move. I did not leave my district and the city of Zagreb for a centimetre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember what the conditions exactly say, that you should remain within the confines of your residence, not the whole of the area, tens of kilometres wide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the police spoke to me about movement, they always speak in terms of the district, because our place of residence is a small place, only 5.000 inhabitants. There is a thermal spa there, and there is no police station in the very place where I reside. The nearest one is in Zabok, and it was always my understanding that I was allowed to move within that area. I really didn't mean to violate the terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak, tell me exactly what happened on that day. You did bring your son and wife to Sljeme, to the area where the event took place?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had agreed to meet up there because she was already there with my son. I went up there and we looked at one race.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did she get there, by car?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She had gone there by car. Transportation had been organised for them, and I followed them knowing that they were already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you make any special arrangements for getting there, because -- did you drive with your own car?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I really know those people well, I had left my car at the parking lot in Bistra. And I got a ride in the limo belonging to some service of the city of Zagreb after the ski pist, and then I joined my wife in her car at Bistra and we used her car to get home. We did not spend up there -- I did not spend there more than one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your wife, you said she went there by her own car. When was this all arranged? Was that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that my wife had gotten there by car. You just asked me this for the first time. I said that I had come to join my wife from Zagreb and I said we had done all that for the sake of my son, and I believed that I was remaining within the district of Zagorije.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't at this moment -- since my computer is not working, I can't check what you exactly said on how your wife got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's page 70 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is my computer is not -- I don't have the right -- let me see there. Perhaps -- yes, I've got it. Yes. But let's just -- we'll finish soon. So as far as -- you didn't go there by your own car. So in order to fetch them, you left your car somewhere in the -- on the slopes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the parking lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, for you to fetch them, as presented, is not a correct version of what happened, is it, because as a matter of fact you joined them -- if I -- yes? Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. With all due respect, I do not see the difference between what we wrote and what you are just asking. He fetched them, except that he was not physically able to go up to the top in his car. He just fetched them, and they all returned together. He had earlier said that he had organised transportation for his wife, that his wife had transportation arranged for her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But when you joined them, did you -- when you joined them did, you use your own car at that time or -- you said you used some transportation that was provided for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I had left my own car at the parking lot, and I got a ride from a service car of the Municipal Assembly up to the skiing complex. I joined my wife and son there. I picked them up. We went together to my car and went home. It's all within the Krapina district, the area where I was told by the police I was allowed to move within.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just note, the parking lot is at the foot of the hill. Since traffic was very heavy, it was forbidden for private cars to go up there. Instead, special transportation was organised to the top, so he drove to the foot of the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I checked what you said. You said she had come which by car. Transportation had been organised for them. So that's where I may have made a mistake. I thought it was by their own car. Now, if transportation was organised for them, what caused you to go there to use -- where you couldn't go any further with your car to use other transportation in order to get to them to get them back to your car?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My motivation was my son's love for skiing. He's seriously training, and I really wanted to join them up there and to take them back home afterwards. I did not attend the competition until the end. We looked at two or three races, and after that we went home. My car was waiting down below at the parking lot, and we went home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what you did the year before as well? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last year the situation was similar. I don't remember the details any more. I remember that the two of them went up there several times and went skiing as well and attended the competitions, and I joined them up there very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a question for you, Madam Slokovic. You have reported to have said to the press that it was no violation of the conditions if Mr. Cermak would bring his child to the ski event. That's a HINA report saying that you gave a telephone conversation -- a telephone interview, in which you said that -- if you want me to read it I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary, Your Honour. I did say on that occasion that Mr. Cermak was not imprisoned in his home. The HINA News Agency asked me whether there were any conditions imposed by the Tribunal that would require Mr. Cermak to stay within his home and in Krapinske Toplice, and I said he was not under house arrest. And it was a telephone interview in which I said the fact that he was taking his son skiing or back or going in working hours for a luncheon or stop somewhere on his way home was something I did not believe to be in violation of the Tribunal's orders. It could be our mistake equally, because I never thought that he was required to stay within the four walls at Marticeva street all the time. So if he made a mistake, then it is also due also to our errors in understanding the decision. Our understanding that he was required stay within certain locations, to be accessible to the Tribunal, and not to move without control. All these incidents happened in an atmosphere of holidays with the knowledge that he would soon be going to The Hague. Maybe his attention relaxed a bit, and it is our fault as lawyers that we did not warn him that he was not allowed to leave the premises at Marticeva street where he worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The conditions says, "not on Saturday and Sunday." You would interpret that as including to go on Sunday where you want to go?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, certain not. That was certainly a mistake on Mr. Cermak's part. But when I made that statement, I said that he was not under house arrest because the news reported the terms of his provisional release as if he were under house arrest and not allowed to leave his home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Ms. Slokovic, aren't the conditions of the provisional release that he should stay within the confinement of his residence? That is his house, isn't it? Not his village, not the area, not the province. It says within the confinement of his residence. That is his house, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I think there may be a problem there, because we really didn't understand it that way. I am not exaggerating, and I am not being untruthful or evasive. But we honestly thought that that meant within his place of residence, which is Krapinske Toplice. The language used by the decision is "place of residence." Maybe the problem lies in the way we understand this term. According to our belief, it was his place of residence, not his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Slokovic, and then unannounced visits to see whether he's present, would they then unannounced go to the whole of the village or the whole of the area, and see whether he is present. That is one of the conditions that was in the first Appeals Chambers decision, which says- and the second one, as well - he should allow unannounced visits to check his presence. Wouldn't that mean that you go to someone's house to see whether he's present, rather than to travel through all of the area to see whether he is at the ski event or in a restaurant or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Krapinske Toplice, you cannot travel far. It's a very small place, indeed. And as Mr. Cermak told you, he stayed exclusively at his own home. He has moved part of his business there. He worked from home, and it was on a couple of occasions that he went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I reported to the police every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was only after he was allowed to officially travel to Zagreb occasionally that he went to Zagreb. Before that, he had organised all of his work from home. It must be a misunderstanding. I really did not understand that he was not allowed to leave his home or that he was required to stay in Zagreb solely at Marticeva street.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to say something as well. The interpretation says "witness," but it is Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want to say that if I had known I was not allowed to leave my home, you may be certain I never would have done so. I always reported on a daily basis to the police station covering our district. If you allow me just a few more words. I want to emphasise that it was never my intention to question or second-guess the decisions of this Court. Please, I would really ask the Trial Chamber to view my recent actions in the context of my conduct of the past eight years. I was always consistently cooperative with the Tribunal and always had great respect for it. In 1998, I gave my first statement, my first interview to the investigators of the OTP. At that time, I was under attack from both the politicians and the media that I was not allowed to because the ban was still in force --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak, we are running out of time, and the issue you are raising now is fully dealt with in the submissions by counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say something, Your Honours, in my very own words and to add something else, by your leave. If you don't let me, then -- I mean, really, I honourably treated this court from day one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one more thing. Since Mr. Cermak said the went to Zabok, which was of course in accordance with the decision. Zabok is ten kilometres away from his house, and that is where the police station is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twelve. It's a very small place. Once you're out; you're out of it. You get out of the building, and you're out of the place itself. And all the relevant institutions are not there and not all the relevant institutions are there and, therefore, it doesn't function properly. It is really my responsibility, because it wasn't mine understanding that he had to be within the confines of four walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think Mr. Cermak is blamed at this moment for reporting in Zabok when there was any need to do so. We're running out of time. We're already half an hour late and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm just trying to illustrate the situation. It's a very small place. When you get out, you immediately have to get out of it a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just have two minutes to say something else, as a human being? Just something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to explain to you that over years eight years from the very outset, I cooperated with this Court, that I was under attack, that I shouldn't be doing that, and that I was attacked by the media and by the sphere of politics. And I had my first contacts and interviews with The Hague Tribunal in 1998, and then after that I gave three other statements. I voluntarily surrendered to the Trial Chamber as soon as the indictment was issued. So I did everything in accordance with the law of the Republic of Croatia on The Hague Tribunal. I also gave three other statements to the investigators of the OTP. I voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal once the indictment was issued. From 2004, when I was provisionally released, I fully abided by all the conditions imposed on me by the Court, and there are regular reports of the Croatian police and government to corroborate that. With my behaviour, I showed that I had full respect for the institution of the Tribunal. Your Honours, I truly believe that this isolated incident cannot be considered as contempt on my part, but simply an action taken in an exceptional situation in New Year's and also the fact that I took my child to a skiing event within my district. Once again, Your Honours, I'm saying that I am sorry by that, and that I will continue to abide by all the instructions of the Court. Please forgive me as a human being. Had I had known that I was supposed to be in my home, I would have been in my home. I -- it would really be a tragedy, as a person who from Croatia in the former Yugoslavia contacted and cooperated with the Tribunal in such a way. If I were to be treated as a person who stood in contempt of court, I mean really that would be so wrong. It was really my mistake. I admit that, and I am so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cermak. May I just please ask for the indulgence of the interpreters, and everybody. We're going to ask for just two or three minutes and then we'll come back. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber is not able to reach a final decision on this issue today. As a result, the suspension of the provisional release order stays in place, and the Trial Chamber will meet or reconvene the Chamber again next week to reconsider the matter. In the meantime, the accused will stay in the United Nations Detection Unit until the matter is formally decided in the new week. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: at 7.39 p.m.
